references.text: In [ref:Gen 6:3|Genesis 6:3], the Lord says that His Spirit will not remain in man forever, "for he is flesh." This text suggests the contrast between humanity's fleshly nature and God's Spirit, providing background for Jesus' point that what is born of the flesh is flesh.

[ref:Isa 40:6|Isaiah 40:6] states that "all flesh is grass," emphasizing the transience of the flesh. Jesus' words that what is born of the flesh is flesh point to this same limitation—flesh cannot by itself produce spiritual life.

In [ref:Ezek 36:26-27|Ezekiel 36:26-27], God promises to give a new heart and put His Spirit within His people. This prophecy of spiritual renewal through God's Spirit forms the background for Jesus' teaching that what is born of the Spirit is spirit.

[ref:John 1:13|John 1:13] says that God's children are born "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." This confirms the distinction between fleshly and spiritual birth that Jesus teaches about.

Paul expands in [ref:Rom 8:5-9|Romans 8:5-9] on the contrast between living according to the flesh and living according to the Spirit. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God, while those who have God's Spirit belong to Christ—a continuation of the distinction between flesh and Spirit.

In [ref:1 Cor 15:50|1 Corinthians 15:50], Paul writes that "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God." This reflects Jesus' teaching that fleshly birth alone is insufficient—one needs a spiritual birth to enter God's kingdom.

In [ref:Gal 4:29|Galatians 4:29], Paul distinguishes between the one born "according to the flesh" (Ishmael) and the one born "according to the Spirit" (Isaac). This typology illustrates the same principle Jesus teaches about fleshly versus spiritual birth.

In [ref:Gal 6:8|Galatians 6:8], Paul writes that whoever sows to the flesh will reap corruption, but whoever sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life. This underscores the radical distinction between flesh and Spirit that Jesus speaks of.
[ref:Ps 51:7|Psalms 51:7] confesses that "in sin I was born," emphasizing that natural, fleshly birth is marked by sin. This points to the need for a new, spiritual birth as Jesus teaches.
